sn11.10:1.2: This opening is reminiscent of [ud1.10](), which specifies the location as Suppāraka
sn11.10:1.5: The sages may have been virtuous, but they were not above a little realpolitik.
sn11.10:1.7: A barbarian (_dāsa_) who “fancied himself godlike” (Rig Veda 7.18.20), Śambara’s 99 mountain forts were destroyed for their bounty (6.47.23) by Indra on behalf of Divodāsa Atithigva (4.26.3). His mention close to Virocana ([sn11.8]()) fits the Arthaśāstra, where they are both invoked together (14.3.19). Despite his decisive defeat at the hands of Indra, later legend makes him a formidable foe and master of sorcery (see [sn11.23]()).
sn11.10:5.5: _Tāta_ (“my dear”) here is an endearment of pity (“oh hon”).
sn11.10:6.2: This inverts the power of his magic to put people to sleep (Arthaśāstra 14.3.19).
